source_text: Si quis dicit corpus Christi esse inanimatum, aut sine mente; et non confitetur ipsum perfectum esse hominem per omnia unum et eundem; anathema esto. Qua ratione potest ullus dicere, corpus Christi esse sine anima, aut mente? Turbatio enim, et dolor, et pavor, neque carnis sunt inanimatae, nec animae non intelligentis; neque divinitatis immutabilis; nec ostensio inanis apparitionis; neque infirmitatis humanae succumbentis defectus: sed passiones naturae nostrae in seipso Verbum ostendebat, suscipiens partem ad patiendum datam. Sicut scriptum est: Quoniam ipse infirmitates nostras assumpsit, et languores nostros ipse tulit. Turbatio enim, et dolor, et pavor, languores animae sunt: defatigatio autem, et somnus, et vulneratio corporis, infirmitates carnis sunt.
thought_title: Christ's body and soul are complete, and his sufferings are real human passions
orientation: Gregory continues his anathemas against errors about Christ's humanity, here rejecting the claim that Christ's body is inanimate or mindless, and showing that his recorded emotions and bodily weaknesses are genuine human passions the Word assumed.
pass_a_gloss: If anyone says the body of Christ is inanimate, or without a mind; and does not confess that he is a complete human being in all respects one and the same; let him be anathema. By what reasoning can anyone say the body of Christ is without a soul, or without a mind? For disturbance, and grief, and fear are neither of an inanimate flesh, nor of a non-intelligent soul; nor of the immutable divinity; nor a display of an empty appearance; nor a defect of human weakness giving way: but the Word was showing the passions of our nature in himself, taking up a portion given for suffering. Just as it is written: For he himself took up our infirmities, and he himself bore our sicknesses. For disturbance, and grief, and fear are sicknesses of the soul: but weariness, and sleep, and wounding are infirmities of the flesh.

choices.why: Glossary bans 'not created' and 'without beginning' for increatum; here inanimatum means lacking a soul, so 'inanimate' is the literal sense.
Literal rendering of the prepositional phrase; 'mindless' would be an adjective but the source uses a phrase.
Matches the range of emotional agitation in the context of Christ's passion; 'trouble' is possible but less precise for the Latin term.
Keeps the literal force of ostensio (showing/display) and inanis (empty/vain) and apparitionis (appearance); avoids collapsing into 'mere phantom'.
Succumbere is to sink under, yield, give way; 'defect of succumbing' is awkward in English, so 'defect of giving way' captures the sense.
The text explicitly glosses its own terms: 'languores animae sunt'; 'sicknesses' matches the citation language from Isaiah/Matthew via the Vulgate 'languores'.

bible_refs.note: Quoniam ipse infirmitates nostras assumpsit, et languores nostros ipse tulit

pass_b_english: If anyone says that the body of Christ is inanimate or without a mind, and does not confess that he is a perfect human being in every respect, one and the same, let him be anathema.

How could anyone say that the body of Christ is without a soul or without a mind? Disturbance, pain, and fear belong neither to inanimate flesh nor to a mindless soul; nor do they belong to the unchanging divinity; nor are they a display of an empty appearance; nor are they a defect of giving way in human weakness. Rather, the Word was showing in himself the sufferings of our nature, taking up a portion given for suffering. As it is written: "For he himself has taken up our infirmities and borne our sicknesses." Disturbance, pain, and fear are sicknesses of the soul; exhaustion, sleep, and wounding are infirmities of the flesh.

problems.quote: Surely he has borne our sicknesses and carried our sorrows.
problems.source_quote: Quoniam ipse infirmitates nostras assumpsit, et languores nostros ipse tulit.
problems.why: Renders infirmitates as 'sicknesses' and languores as 'sorrows' (and Quoniam as 'Surely'), swapping the terms with the next sentence, which calls languores 'sicknesses' and infirmitates 'infirmities'.
problems.fix: For he himself has taken up our infirmities and borne our sicknesses.
problems.ruling: Quote renders infirmitates as sicknesses and languores as sorrows, but the Latin immediately defines languores as soul sicknesses and infirmitates as flesh infirmities—terms misaligned.

edits.old: Surely he has borne our sicknesses and carried our sorrows.
edits.new: For he himself has taken up our infirmities and borne our sicknesses.

fixed: Fixed quotation to match source words "Quoniam ipse infirmitates nostras assumpsit, et languores nostros ipse tulit": Quoniam as For, infirmitates as infirmities, languores as sicknesses, consistent with next sentence.
